What I’m sharing is the same thing I tell all of the people I know in my personal life when the conversation arises. If you truly care the best advice you can give her is to make sure that her end of life wishes are 100% known, completely understood by her husband, and doctors. Cancer is awful, the treatments are equally awful. Going all-in with life sustaining interventions against a condition with a guaranteed poor outcome appears from my emotionally detached rational perspective to be a slow purgatory-hell.

She needs to discuss life saving measures with her doctors, oncologists, everyone she is seeing. She needs to understand what it means to be intubated, on a ventilator, fed through a feeding tube, a tracheostomy. Understand that CPR is traumatic, violent and when done effectively results in broken bones. She may want these things, she may not, but she needs a real explanation about all of it. Almost more important is that her husband to be there for all of these conversations and to understand her wishes.

I have been in situations where an individual has an acute turn for the worst(becoming no longer table to make their own decisions), and in the emotionally charged heat of the moment the family decides to reverse all wishes set forth by the patient. Some doctors thankfully have stood their ground, advocated for the patient and honored their wishes. Others cave to the family and we watch them slowly rot away over days/weeks losing every shred of humanity and dignity knowing there is no hope for recovery.
